evidence.quote: Mini Artichokes: Selective Arbitration of Repeated LLM Disagreement

Repeated inference can improve large-language-model (LLM) reasoning, but correlated agreement is not proof and unconstrained self-correction can damage an initially correct answer. We study whether answer overlap can instead serve as a narrow, gold-free trigger for selective arbitration. Mini Artichokes draws three independent complete-file solutions. It retains the first draw by default and invokes an anonymous judge only when the second and third draws agree with each other and disagree with the first. The judge chooses between the two existing candidates and cannot synthesize a new answer. Our support-aware variant shows the same candidates and anonymous rotation as a matched generic judge, adding only the mechanical one-versus-two support count and a warning that consensus is not proof.

We froze the policy before evaluation on two disjoint, category-proportional 1,000-question samples from MMLU-Pro. The first sample was scored before the second was generated; no policy, prompt, model, fallback, or statistic changed between samples. Pooled over 2,000 questions, support-aware Mini Artichokes scored 1,214/2,000 (60.70%) versus 1,187/2,000 (59.35%) for a direct Luna draw: +27 correct, 33 rescues, 6 harms, one-sided exact McNemar p=7.15e-6, and a 20,000-sample paired-bootstrap 95% confidence interval of +0.75 to +1.95 percentage points. This passes the pre- frozen two-look alpha=.025 boundary. The method was numerically highest but not significantly better than three-draw majority voting (1,209/2,000; p=.0898) or a compute-matched generic judge (1,211/2,000; p=.2539). It required four complete-file model calls and 3.53 times the tokens of direct Luna. A separate 464-case Korean legal-outcome reserve produced the opposite result, identifying a boundary where answer agreement was not informative. The evidence supports selective arbitration as a statistically reliable improvement over direct inference on the tested multiple-choice benchmark, while leaving the incremental value and cross-domain generality of support annotation unresolved.
Keywords: large language models; test-time compute; self-consistency; selective prediction; arbitration; multiple- choice reasoning

Language models often revise their own answers at inference time. Such revision is appealing because it needs neither additional training nor an external verifier. Self-Refine, for example, alternates feedback and revision with the same underlying model [1]. Yet intrinsic self-correction is unreliable on reasoning tasks: models can fail to locate their own mistakes, accept false criticisms, or replace a correct answer with an incorrect one [2-4]. The central problem is therefore not merely how to spend more inference, but how to decide when internally generated evidence is strong enough to authorize a change.

Repeated sampling provides a different source of information. Standard self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and returns the modal answer [5]. Universal Self-Consistency (USC) replaces answer extraction with an LLM selector for free-form outputs [6]. Multi-agent debate and verifier reranking also compare several candidates before selecting an answer [7, 8]. These methods show that diversity and selection can outperform a single trajectory. They do not, however, make agreement infallible. Same-model samples share training data, inductive biases, prompts, and systematic misconceptions; several agents may confidently repeat the same error.

Mini Artichokes tests a conservative use of agreement. It does not replace a base answer whenever a majority appears. It first uses a mechanical overlap event to identify a small conflict set: two independent auxiliary draws agree with one another and disagree with a preassigned base draw. Only those cases are sent to an anonymous judge, and all other cases retain the base. This separates two possible roles for overlap:

evidence.quote: The contributions are empirical and deliberately bounded. First, we define an executable selective-arbitration policy with a gold-free trigger, anonymous candidate rotation, no-synthesis judge, and base-preserving fallback. Second, we evaluate it with two disjoint 1,000-question samples, a policy-unchanged replication, paired exact tests, confidence intervals, and an explicit multiplicity boundary. Third, we isolate the effects of consensus and generic judgment, disclose the complete compute asymmetry, and report a negative legal boundary condition. evidence.section: 2. evidence: the judge may use the number of supporting draws when choosing

evidence.quote: Self-Refine showed that a single model can generate feedback and iteratively revise its output across diverse tasks without additional training [1]. This positive result motivated many inference-time feedback loops. Reasoning tasks also expose a serious limitation. Huang et al. found that models generally did not improve reasoning through intrinsic self- correction without external feedback and sometimes degraded [2]. Stechly et al. reported limitations in self-verification across reasoning and planning [3], while Valmeekam et al. found that LLM self-critique could reduce planning performance relative to sound external verification [4]. Mini Artichokes does not ask a model to revise its own rationale repeatedly. It limits correction to a discrete choice between two already generated answers and defaults to no change.

Self-consistency samples diverse chain-of-thought paths and marginalizes over their final answers [5]. It is a natural strong baseline for stable-answer reasoning tasks. USC generalizes selection to outputs for which deterministic answer extraction is difficult by asking an LLM to select the most consistent candidate [6]. Mini Artichokes shares their use of repeated samples but differs in its asymmetric operating point: D1 is fixed as the base, D2 and D3 only trigger review when they agree against D1, and a judge may still retain D1. Thus, consensus authorizes review rather than automatically authorizing a switch.

Multi-agent debate lets several model instances exchange arguments before a final answer is selected [7]. Training verifiers to rank many sampled solutions can also improve mathematical reasoning [8]. Our setting uses no trained reward model, debate transcript, external execution result, or gold feedback. The arbitration judge sees the original multiple-choice question and two anonymous candidate answers. The matched GJ3/OJ3 comparison is intended to separate ordinary candidate judgment from the additional support annotation.

The closest interpretation of Mini Artichokes is a selective ensemble with an LLM tie-breaker. Its novelty claim is not that multiple samples or LLM judges are new. The contribution is the preassigned-base conflict policy and its controlled evidence: same conflict set, same anonymous candidates, same judge budget, full-denominator paired statistics, unchanged replication, and an explicit negative domain boundary. The experiments also revise the original mechanistic intuition. Agreement is supported as a routing signal on MMLU-Pro; its incremental value as judge-side evidence is not statistically established.

Let a multiple-choice problem be x=(q,A), where q is the question and A=(a1,...,aK) contains K≤10 answer options. A model session returns free text, which is mapped deterministically to one option index. An unmapped response is invalid and is counted wrong in evaluation.

Three independent sessions of the same solver and configuration produce D1(x), D2(x), and D3(x). The draw roles are fixed before any answer is scored: D1 is the base, and D2/D3 are auxiliary draws. No draw is selected as the base after inspecting its quality.
Define the eligible conflict indicator as C(x)=1 when D1, D2, and D3 are all valid and D2=D3≠D1; otherwise C(x)=0.
The conflict is computed without access to gold labels. On C(x)=0, both judge arms return D1. On C(x)=1, the two candidate answers are the base b=D1 and consensus candidate c=D2=D3.
D1 (direct Luna). Return the preassigned first draw.

SC3 (three-draw self-consistency). Return any valid option supported by at least two draws; if there is no majority, return D1. When all three draws are valid, SC3 differs from D1 exactly on eligible conflicts. It can also differ when D1 is invalid and valid D2 and D3 agree. A post hoc boundary audit found no such row in confirmation 1 and two in replication 2; the consensus answer was wrong on both, as was invalid D1, so strict all-valid gating would leave every reported score and comparison unchanged.

GJ3 (matched generic judge). On eligible conflicts, rotate (b) and (c) deterministically into anonymous labels C1/C2. A fourth independent Luna session receives the question and the two candidates and must return one candidate exactly. It is not told which is the base or how many draws support either candidate. Invalid output retains D1.

OJ3 uses the same eligible IDs, anonymous candidate strings, rotation, model, reasoning effort, call count, and fallback as GJ3. It adds only a mechanical support record stating that one anonymous candidate has one complete-file draw and the other has two. Its instruction explicitly says that independent agreement is a fallible signal rather than proof. The judge must solve or check the question, may use the support count as a prior, and cannot create a third answer.

This design prevents three common confounds. It does not search thresholds after scoring, it does not expose candidate provenance, and it does not let the judge improve an answer by synthesizing new content. Comparing OJ3 with GJ3 isolates the support annotation conditional on the same trigger and candidate-selection opportunity.

OJ3 is not described as a validated proof system. “Support-aware” refers only to the number of independent complete- file draws producing an answer. The system makes no claim that the draws are statistically independent at the model level; they are separate sessions of the same model and can share systematic errors. The base-preserving fallback is a policy choice whose net value must be measured through paired rescues and harms.
MMLU-Pro is a 14-category, up-to-ten-option benchmark designed to contain more reasoning-focused and discriminative questions than MMLU [9]. We used the official TIGER-Lab test parquet at Git commit
b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be. Its SHA-256 was 0e24a191...c1ecb9ad8 and it contained 12,032 rows.

Question selection was deterministic, category proportional, and independent of the answer and chain-of-thought fields. Within category, rows were ranked by a fixed-seed SHA hash. Confirmation 1 used ranks 0-999. After that cohort was completely scored, replication 2 was frozen as the immediately following category-proportional allocation, equivalent to cumulative ranks 1,000-1,999. The two public ID sets have intersection zero and union size 2,000. Public question files and private gold files were stored separately, and private gold was not mounted into any model workspace.

Every semantic arm used gpt-5.6-luna with high reasoning effort through the Codex command-line runtime. Each D1- D3 draw processed all 1,000 public rows in one isolated complete-file session. Sessions could read the immutable input file and use a local shell for parsing and arithmetic, but network access, web search, retrieval, memories, plugins, applications, MCP services, and multi-agent delegation were disabled. Candidate sessions could not read one another's outputs. GJ3 and OJ3 were each one additional complete-file session over the frozen conflict set. Provider temperature was neither exposed nor user-configurable in this runtime. No model training or fine-tuning occurred, so training hyperparameters are not applicable.

The whole-file design measures an agentic batch-solving regime rather than independent per-question API calls. It permits cache reuse and within-session context effects. We therefore report actual calls, input, cached input, output/reasoning tokens, elapsed time, invalid mappings, and all accepted receipts. These execution records establish what ran but do not count as scientific performance. The two cohorts used independently initialized whole-file sessions on different questions; they do not constitute repeated executions on the same items. Consequently, the paired tests below quantify item-level uncertainty conditional on the realized sessions, not between-session variance of the complete pipeline.

Confirmation 1 contained 1,000 questions and 14 eligible conflicts. It showed OJ3 601 versus D1 597 (5 rescues, 1 harm; one-sided p=.1094). Because the direction was favorable but underpowered, we froze exactly one disjoint 1,000- question replication. We did not change any policy, prompt, model, effort, role mapping, conflict rule, fallback, or statistic. No third cohort is allowed under the protocol.

evidence.section: 5.5 Development result and negative legal boundary

evidence.quote: The strongest result is straightforward: the unchanged OJ3 policy improved direct Luna on two disjoint MMLU-Pro samples, and the pooled paired effect passed a conservative two-look threshold. The result is not driven by deleting invalid rows, choosing a better direct draw after scoring, or evaluating only the triggered subset. It is a full-denominator comparison against the preassigned D1 draw.

The experiment also establishes that most of the gain is not uniquely attributable to the support annotation. SC3 and GJ3 both significantly improved over D1. OJ3 was numerically highest, and its decisions were favorable in the small set where it differed from GJ3, but the incremental comparison lacked power. This is scientifically more informative than treating “validated overlap” as a monolithic mechanism: answer agreement is useful for routing, generic question-level judgment is useful for arbitration, and the additional support count remains a candidate mechanism rather than a confirmed one.

The tested policy is most plausible for discrete tasks with stable answer mapping, a unique keyed answer, and enough value per question to justify roughly 3.5 times the inference tokens. It may be useful when an existing base answer should be preserved unless a reproducible conflict appears. It is less appropriate for cheap, high-volume inference; tasks where answers cannot be mapped reliably; or outcome prediction from incomplete evidence.

The legal result is not an incidental null. One plausible explanation is that, for a partial fact pattern, two sessions agree because they make the same unstated assumption rather than because the latent court outcome is determined. The present contrast cannot identify that mechanism, because domain, task, prompt, and label structure changed together. Future routing rules should separately manipulate answer determinacy while holding those factors fixed.

Mini Artichokes avoids a long critique-rewrite loop. Its correction is a selection between fixed candidates, which prevents a judge from introducing a novel third error. The design therefore converts self-correction into selective arbitration. This does not solve the general self-verification problem identified in prior work [2-4], but it reduces the surface on which false critique can act.

The absolute pooled improvement was 1.35 percentage points at 3.53 times D1's tokens. Whether that trade is worthwhile depends on application value and latency. OJ3's judge stage was relatively small once three draws had already been purchased, but the three-draw candidate cost dominated the system. Thus, the method is a fallback or batch-quality policy, not a general efficiency claim. A future system should route before generating all auxiliary draws if a reliable pre-inference uncertainty signal is available.

First, confirmation covers one model, one runtime, and one primary benchmark. MMLU-Pro spans 14 disciplines but remains multiple choice, and benchmark questions may have been present in model training. “Fresh” here means not used for policy development and disjoint between the two samples; it does not mean post-training or contamination-free.

Second, each 1,000-question draw was generated in one complete-file agent session. Answers can be affected by within- session context, cache behavior, file parsing, and local computation. The anomalous D2 result in confirmation 1 (14.5%) demonstrates session-level instability. Although D1 was fixed before scoring and replication 2 recovered on a disjoint

question set, no full pipeline was rerun on identical items. The reported paired p-values and bootstrap intervals therefore condition on the realized sessions and do not estimate between-session repeatability. Per-question independent inference may produce different variance and conflict rates.

Third, the three candidate sessions and the judge use the same model family. Separate sessions do not create model-level independence. Correlated errors remain, as shown by 20/68 MMLU-Pro conflicts where both candidates were wrong and by the legal boundary result.

Fourth, only 68/2,000 questions triggered arbitration. This was sufficient for the direct-Luna comparison but not for a precise OJ3-versus-GJ3 estimate. The support annotation's incremental causal effect is unresolved.

Fifth, compute matching is approximate in tokens rather than exact in cached and uncached cost, wall time, or monetary price. OJ3 and GJ3 have equal semantic call counts and nearly equal observed tokens, but their prompts are not byte- identical because the support record is the treatment.

Sixth, the legal reserve is a useful negative boundary but not a comprehensive domain study. It contains Korean civil and tax cases, uses partial fact patterns, and predicts a binary judicial outcome. It simultaneously changes domain, task, prompt, and label structure relative to MMLU-Pro, so it cannot identify why transfer failed. Five selected records retain a legacy local source label for which reuse metadata was not recoverable. The result should not be generalized to legal question answering with complete statutes and facts.

Finally, the protocol allowed one replication after an interim look and used a Bonferroni-style alpha=.025 boundary. No further cohort can be interpreted as part of the same confirmatory family without a new protocol.

This study evaluates public benchmark questions and locally curated Korean precedent text; it does not recruit human participants. The legal pipeline removed outcome text from model input and minimized direct source metadata, but it did not establish full de-identification of facts. Court decisions can remain re-identifiable through distinctive events, and five selected records have no recoverable reuse metadata beyond a legacy source label. We therefore report only aggregate legal results and do not release those item texts or model outputs pending a separate governance review. The method also increases inference compute by design, consuming 45.97 million tokens across the two OJ3 cohorts. Reporting that cost is necessary because modest accuracy gains can be misleading when their resource burden is hidden. The negative legal result cautions against deploying same-model agreement as a reliability signal in high-stakes decision support without external evidence and domain-specific validation.

Mini Artichokes turns repeated-answer overlap into a selective review trigger rather than a claim of truth. On two disjoint MMLU-Pro samples, the frozen support-aware policy significantly improved a preassigned direct Luna draw and had the highest pooled point estimate among the tested arms. Three-draw majority voting and a compute-matched generic judge captured most of the gain, however, and the incremental support annotation was not statistically established. A negative legal reserve further showed that agreement can become uninformative when the input does not determine a unique outcome. The useful result is therefore narrow: selective arbitration can improve repeated LLM reasoning on the tested multiple-choice regime, provided its compute cost and domain boundary are made explicit.

The double-blind artifact contains the MMLU-Pro public benchmark IDs, deterministic selection code, frozen protocols, exact prompts, accepted candidate and judge outputs, private-score scripts, aggregate reports, and tests. Private gold was kept separate from model workspaces. For the legal reserve, the artifact contains the frozen protocol and aggregate negative boundary statistics only; item texts and outputs are withheld for the governance reasons above. findings.author_question: Can you provide a machine-generated comparison proving that GJ3 and OJ3 differ only in the support-treatment note and associated support field, with identical conflict IDs, candidate strings, rotations, runtime settings, and fallbacks?
findings.claim: The selective-arbitration policy is precisely executable and controls several observable confounds through preassigned draw roles, an all-valid mechanical trigger, anonymous rotation, fixed candidates, and a closely matched generic-judge arm.
findings.falsification_test: This strength is falsified if an artifact-level diff reveals any GJ3/OJ3 difference in eligible rows, candidate text, candidate rotation, model configuration, judge opportunity, or fallback beyond the declared support-treatment package, or if D1 was assigned after scoring.
findings.reasoning: Fixing D1 before scoring prevents post-hoc base selection, while the gold-free trigger and no-synthesis fallback make the algorithm unambiguous. Matching the two judge arms removes obvious candidate-set and compute-opportunity explanations, although it does not by itself address session-level stochastic confounding.
findings.score_impact: Positive—materially supports QUAL-MET by making the policy auditable and its conditional arm comparisons interpretable.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain this design and add the machine-generated arm diff and invariant-check report to the main empirical record.

findings.author_question: Was the complete two-look boundary, one-sided direction, fixed hypothesis sequence, denominator rule, and bootstrap procedure sealed before the first gold scoring, and can a dated protocol artifact substantiate that timing?
findings.claim: The reported inferential protocol is technically coherent: it uses full-denominator paired outcomes, exact discordant-pair tests, a conservative two-look threshold, fixed-sequence testing, and stratified paired bootstrap intervals.
findings.falsification_test: This strength is falsified if the frozen protocol postdates outcome inspection, raw-output recomputation does not reproduce the exact paired tails and intervals, excluded or remapped rows alter the denominator, or formal claims continue past the first unrejected fixed-sequence hypothesis.
findings.reasoning: McNemar's exact tail is appropriate for paired binary outcomes conditional on the realized runs. The alpha=.025 boundary conservatively bounds two-look error without requiring independent looks, and full-denominator scoring avoids conditioning the headline result on triggered cases.
findings.score_impact: Positive—substantially strengthens QUAL-MET for the conditional item-level comparison and limits multiplicity-driven overclaiming.
findings.suggested_fix: Include a dated pre-analysis artifact and a one-command reproduction of all discordance tables, exact tails, sequence decisions, and bootstrap intervals.

findings.author_question: Across independent full-pipeline reruns on the same frozen questions, what is the distribution of OJ3-minus-D1 accuracy and trigger rate, and how would a session anomaly be handled without outcome-dependent exclusion?
findings.claim: The headline item-level inference does not establish repeatability of the stochastic pipeline because each 1,000-item draw is one shared whole-file session, the cohorts use different items, and no identical-item pipeline reruns estimate between-session variance.
findings.falsification_test: Run a preregistered set of independently initialized complete pipelines on identical frozen items. This concern is falsified if a session-clustered or hierarchical analysis shows a stable positive OJ3-minus-D1 effect with uncertainty excluding zero and no material sensitivity to whole-file session realizations.
findings.reasoning: All item outcomes within a draw share the same session-level context, caching, parsing, and execution realization. The 145/1,000 versus 607/1,000 D2 swing demonstrates that this cluster effect can be large. Resampling questions cannot estimate that variance, so the very small McNemar p-value is conditional on the realized sessions rather than evidence of pipeline-level repeatability.
findings.score_impact: Negative—materially limits QUAL-MET and the interpretation of the gain as statistically reliable beyond the two realized batch executions.
findings.suggested_fix: Repeat the full pipeline several times on identical frozen items and analyze items crossed with session replicates, or restrict the claim explicitly to conditional performance of the recorded executions.

findings.author_question: Will you repeat GJ3 and OJ3 under randomized, crossed judge sessions on the same conflict rows so that support treatment is not perfectly coupled to a particular whole-file judge realization?
findings.claim: The OJ3-versus-GJ3 design does not causally isolate support annotation because the treatment is applied at the complete-file judge-session level with only one judge realization per arm and cohort.
findings.falsification_test: Use multiple independent judge sessions under both treatment notes on the same conflict rows, randomize treatment and processing order, and cluster by session and item. The concern is falsified if the support-treatment coefficient remains consistently positive after accounting for judge-session variation.
findings.reasoning: Matching observable inputs is valuable, but GJ3 and OJ3 are separate stochastic whole-file calls. Consequently, their 13 differing choices can reflect the support package, session randomness, or context trajectory. Item-level pairing cannot separate these factors when prompt treatment is effectively assigned to an unreplicated session cluster.
findings.score_impact: Negative—substantially weakens the mechanistic QUAL-MET claim that the comparison isolates support annotation, without invalidating the recorded end-to-end point estimates.
findings.suggested_fix: Run replicated randomized crossover judge calls and estimate the treatment effect with session-clustered or mixed-effects inference; until then, describe the contrast as observational over realized judge sessions.

findings.author_question: What algorithmic capability, guarantee, or reproducible advantage arises uniquely from the preassigned-base/support mechanism that cannot be obtained by SC3 or the matched generic candidate judge?
findings.claim: The methodological novelty is incremental: the paper itself positions the method as a selective ensemble with an LLM tie-breaker, while its distinctive support-aware arm is not established as better than majority voting or the matched generic judge.
findings.falsification_test: This assessment is falsified by either a formal result demonstrating a nontrivial property unavailable to standard self-consistency or generic candidate selection, or a preregistered, adequately powered study showing that the distinctive policy component consistently outperforms both SC3 and GJ3.
findings.reasoning: Repeated sampling, majority selection, and LLM candidate judgment are established ingredients in the paper's own account. The preassigned-base routing rule is a clear operating-point variation, but OJ3 improves SC3 by only 0.25 points and GJ3 by 0.15 points with intervals crossing zero. The evidence therefore supports a carefully evaluated policy composition more strongly than a genuinely new algorithmic advance.
findings.score_impact: Negative—meaningfully limits ORIG-MTH, while leaving intact the value of the controlled empirical policy evaluation.
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow the novelty claim to the asymmetric policy and evaluation design, or add a formal decision-theoretic contribution and a powered test of the component unique to OJ3.

findings.author_question: Can you report cohort-stratified uncertainty for trigger enrichment, the base-versus-consensus contingency, and the five-case advantage from selective base retention?
findings.claim: The conflict-set decomposition is a concrete analytical strength that separates routing utility, candidate-set limitations, and harm avoidance rather than attributing the full accuracy gain to a single mechanism.
findings.falsification_test: Recompute the decomposition from accepted row-level outputs. This strength is falsified if the base, consensus, and both-wrong cells do not partition all 68 conflicts, or if OJ3's reported base-retention decisions do not yield seven base wins versus two consensus wins and hence a net five over SC3.
findings.reasoning: Reporting that consensus was correct on 35 conflicts, the base on 13, and neither on 20 exposes both the routing signal and its ceiling. The decision decomposition also identifies exactly how arbitration avoided five majority errors and appropriately refrains from treating the OJ3-GJ3 increment as causal.
findings.score_impact: Positive—materially supports ORIG-ANL by providing mechanism-relevant empirical insight beyond aggregate accuracy.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the decomposition and add exact or bootstrap uncertainty, stratified by cohort, while retaining its descriptive status.

findings.author_question: Which observable, gold-free predeployment statistic would tell a practitioner that answer overlap is likely to be beneficial rather than harmful in a new task?
findings.claim: The boundary analysis does not yet yield a predictive account of when overlap is useful: its proposed operating conditions are qualitative, and the negative legal contrast changes domain, task, prompt, and label structure simultaneously.
findings.falsification_test: Hold domain, prompt, task, and label structure fixed while experimentally varying answer determinacy or solver-error correlation. This weakness is falsified if those manipulations produce a reproducible, gold-free diagnostic that predicts the sign and magnitude of selective arbitration's net effect on held-out data.
findings.reasoning: The legal reserve successfully refutes a domain-general advantage, but simultaneous changes prevent identification of underdetermination or correlated assumptions as the cause. Conditions such as discrete mapping and a unique keyed answer are plausible descriptors, not an analytical deployment rule or theory of expected gain.
findings.score_impact: Negative—limits ORIG-ANL because the boundary result is diagnostic but not yet an explanatory or predictive insight; it does not undermine the narrow MMLU-Pro result.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a controlled factorial study of determinacy and error correlation and formalize expected rescue-minus-harm conditions that can be estimated without target-domain gold at decision time.

findings.author_question: Can you provide an auditable creation-time chain showing that the replication-2 IDs and unchanged protocol were fixed before its first model call?
findings.claim: The confirmatory design uses deterministic, category-proportional, nonoverlapping cohorts and an unchanged replication after the first look.
findings.falsification_test: Compare the two ID lists and the protocol, prompt, model, role, and statistic manifests across cohorts; any overlapping ID or score-informed change would refute this strength.
findings.reasoning: Label-independent selection, zero cohort overlap, and explicit freezing reduce selection leakage and post hoc policy tuning in the primary evaluation.
findings.score_impact: Positive—materially increases trust in the internal validity of the confirmatory comparison.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a signed or timestamped manifest linking both ID lists, the replication protocol hash, and the first replication receipt; otherwise retain the design unchanged.

findings.author_question: Do the artifacts permit a byte-level comparison showing that GJ3 and OJ3 differ only in the support treatment and warning?
findings.claim: SC3 and the closely compute-matched GJ3 provide strong controls for majority selection and generic candidate judgment.
findings.falsification_test: Diff the conflict IDs, candidate strings, rotations, model settings, fallback behavior, and call records; any material difference beyond the support field and warning would invalidate the claimed isolation.
findings.reasoning: The controls distinguish gains from repeated sampling and ordinary judging from the incremental support annotation, while GJ3 and OJ3 differ by only 0.41% in observed tokens.
findings.score_impact: Positive—substantially strengthens interpretation of the ablation and comparison results.
findings.suggested_fix: Include an automated treatment-diff report or checksums for the matched judge inputs and hidden role maps.

findings.author_question: Was the alpha boundary and fixed sequence recorded before Confirmation 1 was scored, and does the supplied analysis reproduce every reported p-value and interval?
findings.claim: The inferential plan appropriately uses paired tests, stratified paired bootstrap intervals, and explicit two-look and fixed-sequence multiplicity control.
findings.falsification_test: Recompute results from row-level arm outcomes and inspect the dated protocol; mismatched p-values, unpreserved bootstrap strata, or a post-result multiplicity plan would refute this strength.
findings.reasoning: Exact discordant-pair testing matches the paired predictions, full denominators are retained, and the stated stopping rules prevent the unreached GJ3 comparison from becoming a formal claim.
findings.score_impact: Positive—materially increases trust in the reported direct-baseline significance result.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the preregistered analysis manifest and provide a deterministic command that regenerates the paired tables, tests, and bootstrap intervals.

findings.author_question: Does the submitted artifact provide a single documented path that regenerates the MMLU-Pro score tables and pooled artifact hash from the accepted outputs and scorer inputs?
findings.claim: The paper provides unusually extensive implementation provenance, including runtime settings, exact prompts, accepted outputs, scoring resources, hashes, and execution receipts.
findings.falsification_test: Audit the artifact manifest and rerun its analysis; missing referenced files, irreproducible tables, or hash mismatches would refute this strength.
findings.reasoning: These materials support inspection of selection, arm construction, prompting, parsing, and scoring even though stochastic semantic calls may not replay identically.
findings.score_impact: Positive—raises confidence that the realized experiment and analysis can be independently audited.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a one-command reproduction entry point and immutable runtime or model identifiers where available.

findings.author_question: Across repeated complete-file executions on the same frozen items, how often do session failures like the Confirmation-1 D2 anomaly occur, and does the OJ3-minus-D1 effect remain positive when session variation is included?
findings.claim: Between-session repeatability of the complete pipeline is unestimated despite evidence of a large session-level failure mode.
findings.falsification_test: Repeat every arm multiple times on identical item sets and show stable conflict rates and a session-aware OJ3-minus-D1 interval that remains above zero.
findings.reasoning: Each arm is one whole-file session, yet D2 changed from 145/1,000 to 607/1,000 across cohorts. Item-level paired tests therefore establish the realized-session effect but not the repeatability of the deployed stochastic pipeline.
findings.score_impact: Negative—substantially limits reliance on the significant item-level result as evidence of a repeatable pipeline gain.
findings.suggested_fix: Run multiple independently initialized full pipelines on the same frozen items and report session-level effect, conflict-rate, and failure distributions using hierarchical or cluster-aware uncertainty.

findings.author_question: What incremental effect over SC3 or GJ3 was the design powered to detect given that only 3.4% of questions triggered arbitration?
findings.claim: OJ3 does not establish improvement over either strong multi-call control, so the incremental support-aware mechanism is unconfirmed.
findings.falsification_test: Under a new preregistered protocol, obtain enough discordant conflicts for multiplicity-controlled intervals to exclude zero for OJ3 versus both SC3 and GJ3.
findings.reasoning: The estimated gains are only +0.25 points over SC3 and +0.15 over GJ3, with both confidence intervals crossing zero and respective one-sided p-values of .08984 and .25391.
findings.score_impact: Negative—prevents credit for a demonstrated support-annotation or state-of-the-art improvement; only superiority to direct D1 is supported.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the headline claim restricted to direct inference, or conduct a new study sized by expected triggered and discordant cases if mechanism superiority is central.

findings.author_question: Can you release a hashed aggregate paired contingency table and pre-freeze record for the legal reserve without exposing sensitive item text?
findings.claim: The adverse Korean legal result is valuable negative evidence that directly bounds any domain-general agreement claim.
findings.falsification_test: Recompute the frozen reserve outcomes; failure to reproduce OJ3's 30 rescues, 59 harms, and 32/65 supported-outcome accuracy, or evidence of outcome-informed reserve selection, would negate this strength.
findings.reasoning: OJ3 fell from P1's 61.21% to 54.96%, and the supported outcome was correct only 49.2% of the time. Reporting this result separately rather than pooling it usefully constrains transfer claims.
findings.score_impact: Positive—adds decision-relevant negative evidence and improves the credibility of the paper's bounded conclusions.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the negative result and add reproducible aggregate paired tables, protocol hashes, and selection-audit summaries.

findings.author_question: Which changed factor is hypothesized to drive the legal failure, and is there a matched experiment that varies that factor while holding the others fixed?
findings.claim: The novel legal-boundary setup cannot identify why transfer failed because domain, task, prompt, label structure, and answer determinacy changed together.
findings.falsification_test: Construct matched conditions that manipulate determinacy while holding domain, task, prompt, and labels fixed; a stable isolated effect would support the proposed mechanism.
findings.reasoning: The reserve establishes non-transfer in that setting but cannot distinguish shared assumptions under partial observation from the other simultaneous shifts.
findings.score_impact: Negative—reduces the mechanistic and benchmark value of the novel boundary setup, without undermining its descriptive negative result or the core MMLU-Pro finding.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a matched or factorial boundary study that varies input completeness or outcome determinacy independently of domain, prompt, and label format.

findings.author_question: Will the title, abstract, and any submission summary consistently present the contribution as selective arbitration rather than imply that support annotation itself was validated?
findings.claim: The paper communicates its evidential boundary unusually clearly: it distinguishes the supported OJ3-over-D1 result from the unrejected strong-control comparisons, discloses the compute multiplier, and foregrounds the negative legal boundary.
findings.falsification_test: This strength would be falsified by any headline or concluding statement that asserts support-annotation superiority, efficiency, or domain-general transfer without the qualifications stated in these blocks.
findings.reasoning: The abstract, paired-results discussion, and conclusion repeat the same narrow interpretation instead of allowing the highest point estimate to become an unsupported mechanism claim.
findings.score_impact: Positive: materially strengthens writing quality and claim calibration.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve this wording discipline and ensure captions, metadata, and any supplemental summary use the same bounded claim.

findings.author_question: Can Table 2 include a compact fixed-sequence-status field so readers cannot mistake the descriptive OJ3-versus-GJ3 value for a formally reached test?
findings.claim: Table 2 is decision-informative because it places rescues, harms, net correctness, the one-sided exact test, and confidence-interval bounds together on the full pooled denominator.
findings.falsification_test: Reconstruct every row from the reported discordances and denominator; this strength fails if the net effects, p-values, interval units, or comparison identities cannot be recovered unambiguously.
findings.reasoning: The table exposes both improvements and harms and lets readers distinguish the reliable D1 comparison from the uncertain SC3 and GJ3 increments without relying only on aggregate accuracy.
findings.score_impact: Positive but bounded: improves visual communication of the central evidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the paired layout and add a column marking each comparison as rejected, reached but unrejected, or descriptive only.

findings.author_question: Is the intended originality claim attached to the complete routing-and-arbitration policy or specifically to the support-count treatment?
findings.claim: The work offers a creative, well-motivated combination of known components: a preassigned base, a two-against-one conflict trigger, anonymous candidate rotation, a no-synthesis judge, a base-preserving fallback, and a matched generic-judge control.
findings.falsification_test: A closest-work comparison demonstrating a prior method with the same asymmetric trigger, fallback, anonymous constrained judge, and matched support-hidden control would falsify this synthesis claim.
findings.reasoning: The paper explicitly disclaims novelty for repeated sampling and LLM judging while identifying the policy composition and controlled isolation as its contribution.
findings.score_impact: Positive: supports meaningful originality credit for synthesis despite familiar individual ingredients.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the novelty statement centered on the complete policy and controlled evaluation; avoid presenting the unconfirmed support-count effect as the novel result.

findings.author_question: What concrete multiple-choice or batch-quality setting makes 27 additional correct answers per 2,000 queries valuable enough to motivate adoption?
findings.claim: Within the tested MMLU-Pro regime, the unchanged policy shows credible domain-specific importance through a positive replication and a pooled full-denominator gain of 27 correct answers over direct Luna.
findings.falsification_test: Recompute both cohort and pooled paired outcomes from the released score artifact; this strength fails if the replication is not positive or the reported +27, discordances, p-value, or interval do not reproduce.
findings.reasoning: The effect is modest but replicated, evaluated on the full denominator, and supported by paired uncertainty estimates rather than only a triggered-subset analysis.
findings.score_impact: Positive: raises the demonstrated significance within repeated multiple-choice reasoning.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one concrete domain-use scenario and translate the effect into an interpretable rate such as extra correct answers per 1,000 questions.

findings.author_question: Given the unrejected OJ3-versus-SC3 comparison and unreached OJ3-versus-GJ3 test, should the central contribution be framed as routing plus constrained arbitration rather than support-aware arbitration?
findings.claim: Broad significance is limited because the support annotation—the feature distinguishing OJ3 from the matched generic judge—has no established incremental advantage, and only 68 of 2,000 items triggered arbitration.
findings.falsification_test: A preregistered, adequately powered evaluation showing OJ3 consistently outperforming both SC3 and GJ3 across additional models and task families would falsify this limitation.
findings.reasoning: Most observed improvement is already captured by majority voting or generic judging, while the distinctive support treatment is estimated from few informative disagreements.
findings.score_impact: Negative: materially constrains broad research impact and the significance attributable to the named support-aware mechanism.
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow headline claims to the demonstrated routing-and-arbitration result, or add powered multi-model and multi-task comparisons before claiming a broader support-aware advance.

findings.author_question: Can the authors report monetary cost, measured or bounded energy use, and cost per additional correct answer for the tested runtime?
findings.claim: Real-world impact remains difficult to assess because the 1.35-point gain requires 3.53 times D1's tokens, while token matching does not establish monetary, latency, or environmental cost.
findings.falsification_test: Measured deployment cost and energy data, together with an application-specific value threshold showing an acceptable cost per corrected answer, would falsify this practical-impact limitation.
findings.reasoning: The paper responsibly discloses token use, but tokens alone do not permit a societal or operational cost-benefit judgment, particularly across providers or deployment settings.
findings.score_impact: Negative: reduces the demonstrated real-world significance without undermining the benchmark result itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Report monetary and energy estimates or defensible ranges, latency distributions, and an explicit cost-per-extra-correct calculation.

findings.author_question: What reuse authorization or governance determination covered the five legacy lawlaw records, and will they be excluded if that basis cannot be recovered?
findings.claim: The legal reserve has an unresolved data-governance issue because five processed records lack recoverable reuse metadata, while narrative facts retain residual re-identification risk.
findings.falsification_test: Recovering valid provenance and reuse terms for all five records, or excluding them and documenting an unchanged aggregate analysis under an approved governance process, would falsify this concern.
findings.reasoning: Withholding item-level text limits further disclosure but does not itself resolve whether processing records with unknown reuse terms was authorized.
findings.score_impact: Negative: creates a material data-usage and privacy-compliance concern that may affect use or release of the legal analysis.
findings.suggested_fix: Quarantine or remove the five records pending provenance review, rerun the aggregate legal analysis, and document the applicable licenses and governance approval.

findings.author_question: Will the final submission map this discussion explicitly to the venue's required ethics, societal-impact, and environmental checklist items?
findings.claim: The paper provides a substantive impact disclosure: it identifies residual legal-data re-identification risk, withholds sensitive artifacts pending governance review, reports the compute burden, and warns against high-stakes use without external validation.
findings.falsification_test: This strength would fail if the venue requires an omitted disclosure, if legal item-level material is released before governance clearance, or if deployment claims contradict the stated high-stakes warning.
findings.reasoning: The discussion connects affected data subjects, privacy risk, resource burden, and deployment harm to concrete mitigations rather than offering a generic impact statement.
findings.score_impact: Positive: meaningfully strengthens responsible-AI and broader-impact compliance, while not curing the separate provenance issue.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the section, add the formal governance-review status and venue-checklist mapping, and keep the high-stakes deployment caveat prominent.

ethical_concerns.details: Verified ethical concerns: Five selected legacy lawlaw records lack recoverable reuse metadata, and the transformations do not comprehensively de-identify narrative facts, leaving residual re-identification risk; item-level materials are withheld pending governance review.

key_questions.assessment_change: Stable effects and conflict rates across identical-item repetitions would raise the soundness score and overall acceptance assessment by addressing unestimated pipeline repeatability; substantial sensitivity to session realization would lower both.
key_questions.question: Can the authors repeat the complete pipeline on the same MMLU-Pro items and report between-session variation in D1 accuracy, trigger rate, OJ3-versus-D1 effects, and OJ3-versus-GJ3 effects?

key_questions.assessment_change: A reproducible positive OJ3-versus-GJ3 effect under repeated paired or counterbalanced judge sessions would raise the soundness, originality, and significance scores and strengthen acceptance by supporting an incremental support-annotation effect; a null or session-sensitive result would not support that mechanism.
key_questions.question: Can GJ3 and OJ3 be evaluated over multiple paired or counterbalanced judge sessions on the same frozen conflicts, with the support record as the only treatment difference?

key_questions.assessment_change: Deployment-level evidence showing a favorable accuracy–cost trade-off would raise the significance score and overall acceptance assessment; evidence that monetary cost or latency dominates the 1.35-point gain would lower them.
key_questions.question: Can the authors report cached and uncached monetary costs and deployment-relevant latency for the 1.35-percentage-point gain, rather than token totals alone?

key_questions.assessment_change: A matched experiment identifying an effect of answer determinacy would raise the originality and significance scores and strengthen acceptance by providing a predictive boundary for the method; failure to isolate such an effect would leave the generalization assessment limited.
key_questions.question: Can the authors test answer determinacy while holding domain, task, prompt, and label structure fixed to isolate the proposed explanation for the negative legal result?

key_questions.assessment_change: Documenting a valid reuse basis or removing the affected records, together with specified governance and re-identification safeguards, could improve the ethical acceptability and overall acceptance assessment; unresolved reuse status and residual risk would sustain the concern and could lower acceptance.
key_questions.question: Can the authors establish a reuse basis for the five legacy records or exclude them, and specify the governance criteria and re-identification review required before any item-level release?

review.limitations: Confirmation covers one model, one runtime, and one primary multiple-choice benchmark; the benchmark may have appeared in model training, and “fresh” does not mean post-training or contamination-free. [ev_p007_b015] The pipeline was not rerun on identical items, so the paired inference conditions on the realized whole-file sessions and does not estimate between-session repeatability; the large D2 discrepancy across cohorts raises a repeatability concern without establishing its cause. [ev_p004_b009] [ev_p005_b007] [ev_p008_b002] All candidate and judge sessions use the same model family, so separate sessions do not remove correlated model-level errors; both available candidates were wrong on 20 of 68 conflicts. [ev_p008_b003] Only 68 of 2,000 questions triggered arbitration, limiting precision for the OJ3-versus-GJ3 comparison and leaving the incremental support-annotation effect unresolved. [ev_p008_b004] The legal reserve changes domain, task, prompt, and label structure simultaneously, so it cannot identify why transfer failed or support conclusions about legal question answering with complete statutes and facts. [ev_p008_b006]
strengths: The paper clearly positions its contribution as an asymmetric preassigned-base routing-and-arbitration policy, with a matched support-hidden judge control rather than a claim that repeated sampling or LLM judging is itself new. [ev_p002_b014] [ev_p003_b013] [ev_p003_b016]

OJ3 and GJ3 share eligible conflicts, anonymous candidate strings, rotation, model settings, semantic call count, and fallback, with the mechanical support record as the stated treatment difference. [ev_p003_b013] [ev_p013_b002]

The confirmatory cohorts are deterministically selected, category-proportional, and disjoint; the replication preserves the policy and analysis choices, while gold labels remain outside solver and judge workspaces. [ev_p004_b006] [ev_p004_b011] [ev_p011_b022]

The analysis uses full-denominator accuracy, paired exact discordance tests, stratified paired-bootstrap intervals, and a pre-frozen fixed testing sequence with a stopping rule. [ev_p004_b014] [ev_p004_b015] [ev_p004_b016] [ev_p004_b017] [ev_p004_b018] [ev_p004_b019] [ev_p004_b020]

The pooled comparison table places rescues, harms, net correctness, exact-test results, and confidence-interval bounds together, making the main comparisons easy to assess. [ev_p005_b019] [ev_p005_b020] [ev_p005_b021] [ev_p005_b022] [ev_p005_b023] [ev_p005_b024]

The conflict-set analysis separates routing utility, candidate-set failures, and avoided consensus harms while explicitly declining to attribute the OJ3-versus-GJ3 increment causally to support counts. [ev_p006_b004] [ev_p006_b005] [ev_p006_b013]
review.summary: The paper studies OJ3, a selective-arbitration policy with D1 fixed as the base and D2/D3 as auxiliary draws. Review occurs only when all three answers are valid and D2 and D3 agree against D1; an anonymous judge then selects one existing candidate, and OJ3 adds a one-versus-two support record relative to GJ3. [ev_p003_b005] [ev_p003_b006] [ev_p003_b011] [ev_p003_b013] Evaluation uses two disjoint, category-proportional 1,000-question MMLU-Pro cohorts, with an unchanged replication after the first look, full-denominator scoring, and a conservative one-sided alpha of .025 for the pooled headline test. [ev_p004_b006] [ev_p004_b011] [ev_p004_b012] [ev_p004_b014] Pooled OJ3 accuracy was 1,214 of 2,000 versus 1,187 of 2,000 for D1, a gain of 27 correct answers from 33 rescues and six harms; the 1.35-point effect had one-sided p=7.15e-6 and a 95% interval of +0.75 to +1.95 points. [ev_p005_b010] [ev_p005_b015] [ev_p005_b017] [ev_p014_b035]
weaknesses: OJ3 did not establish superiority over SC3 or GJ3: its five-answer advantage over SC3 was not rejected, the GJ3 comparison was not formally reached, and the observed three-answer GJ3 difference was nonsignificant. [ev_p005_b018] [ev_p014_b036] [ev_p014_b037] [ev_p008_b004]

Because GJ3 and OJ3 each used one separate complete-file judge session, their realized contrast cannot distinguish the support-record treatment from judge-session or within-session context variation. [ev_p003_b016] [ev_p004_b008] [ev_p004_b009] [ev_p006_b006]

The practical gain is modest relative to compute: the 1.35-point improvement over D1 required 3.53 times its tokens, while token matching does not establish exact monetary cost or wall-time latency. [ev_p006_b015] [ev_p007_b013] [ev_p008_b005]

The proposed operating boundary remains qualitative, and the negative legal comparison cannot provide a predictive explanation because domain, task, prompt, and label structure all changed together. [ev_p007_b002] [ev_p007_b008] [ev_p007_b009] [ev_p008_b006]

verdicts.effective_claim: The described construction preassigns D1 before scoring, uses an all-valid mechanical conflict trigger, anonymizes and rotates the two fixed candidates, and states that GJ3 and OJ3 share eligible IDs, candidate strings, runtime settings, call count, and fallback, differing only in OJ3's support-treatment package.

evidence_verdict.narrowed_claim: The described construction preassigns D1 before scoring, uses an all-valid mechanical conflict trigger, anonymizes and rotates the two fixed candidates, and states that GJ3 and OJ3 share eligible IDs, candidate strings, runtime settings, call count, and fallback, differing only in OJ3's support-treatment package.
evidence_verdict.rationale: The cited blocks directly establish each design premise: preassigned draw roles (ev_p003_b005), the all-valid trigger (ev_p003_b006), matched judge-arm inputs and settings with only a support-record addition (ev_p003_b013), and anonymous deterministic rotation plus the same invariants (ev_p013_b002). These blocks support the sanitized methodological strength. They are textual specifications, however, not the machine-generated artifact-level diff requested in the author question, so they do not independently prove implementation compliance.

impact_verdict.rationale: The method and supplement state that D1 was preassigned and that GJ3/OJ3 shared eligible IDs, candidate strings, rotation, runtime settings, judge opportunity, and fallback; the supplied pseudocode also makes the intended policy executable. Session instability was substantial, inference conditions on realized sessions, compute matching was approximate, and the paper explicitly says the support annotation’s incremental causal effect is unresolved. Thus the intended controls are documented, but the stronger claim that the arms differed only by the declared treatment package is not independently verified.
impact_verdict.reconstructed_issue: The GJ3–OJ3 causal contrast depends on manuscript-level arm-invariance assertions rather than a supplied artifact-level comparison, so undeclared row, configuration, or fallback differences cannot be excluded from this evidence alone.

impact_verdict.rationale: The formulas and reported execution are internally coherent: full-denominator paired scoring, exact one-sided discordant-pair tails, alpha=.025 for two looks, fixed-sequence stopping, and stratified paired bootstrap are described, and the disclosed results respect the stopping rule. However, the first replication was frozen only after observing a favorable first-cohort direction, and the supplied evidence contains no dated pre-analysis artifact showing that the direction, boundary, hypothesis order, denominator rule, and bootstrap procedure were sealed before that inspection. Thus technical coherence is supported, but its confirmatory timing—and therefore the full decision-level strength—remains unresolved rather than contradicted.
